**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I heard my name spoken aloud, it was in a voice I didn’t recognize. My mother’s lips moved, but the sound that came out was foreign—soft, hesitant, like she was testing the shape of it on her tongue. I was three years old, sitting on the floor of our tiny apartment in Madrid, kicking a plastic ball against the wall. She called me *Lucía*, and for a moment, the world tilted. The name was a secret, something she’d kept close to her chest until that day. Now it was out there, floating between us, heavy with meaning.

I didn’t understand then that names aren’t just labels. They’re the first stories we’re given, the first threads that tie us to the people who made us. My mother’s name was *María*, but she never called herself that. She was *Mama*, or *La Chica de los Ojos Verdes*—the girl with green eyes—when she wanted to be remembered. My father’s name was *Javier*, but he was *El Profesor* to strangers, *El Tipo de la Barba* to the bartender at the corner café. Names shift like sand, depending on who’s holding them.

I grew up in a house where names were currency. My mother’s family was from Andalusia, where surnames were passed down like heirlooms, where *González* or *Martínez* could mean as much as a last will and testament. My father’s side was different—Catalan, where names were shorter, sharper, like *Ramon* or *Carme*, names that fit in a single breath. He used to joke that if he had a daughter, he’d call her *Esperanza*—Hope—but he never did. Instead, he gave me *Lucía*, a name that meant "light" in Latin, though he never told me that. Maybe he didn’t know. Maybe he just liked the sound of it.

I was named after my great-grandmother, *Lucía de la Cruz*, who died when my mother was a child. She was a seamstress in Seville, they said, with hands that could stitch a dress in the dark. My mother had a photograph of her—yellowed edges, a woman with a stern face and a cigarette dangling from her lips. She never spoke of her, but I knew. Names are like that. They carry the weight of what’s unsaid.

When I was twelve, I started changing my name. Not legally, not yet—but in my head. I called myself *Luz* sometimes, short for *Lucía*, because it sounded lighter, easier. My friends at school called me *Lucy*, which was worse, because it made me feel like I was being stripped of something. I wanted to keep the *ía*, the Spanishness of it, the way it rolled off the tongue like a secret. But I also wanted to be something else. Something new.

That’s when I met Daniel.

He was in my literature class, tall and quiet, with a habit of chewing on the inside of his cheek when he was thinking. He had a way of looking at me that made my stomach flip, like he was seeing something beneath the surface. The first time he spoke to me, he said, *"Tu nombre es bonito."* Your name is beautiful. I almost laughed. Beautiful? My name was just a name. It was a name that had been handed down, a name that belonged to someone who wasn’t even alive anymore.

But he kept saying it. *"Lucía."* Like it was a promise.

We started dating in the summer after graduation. He took me to places I’d never been—old bookstores in Barcelona, rooftop terraces where the city stretched out like a map beneath us. He taught me how to make *paella*, how to dance *sevillanas*, how to say *te quiero* without my voice cracking. He called me *mi luz*, my light, and for the first time, I believed it.

Then he left.

It wasn’t a breakup. It was worse. He just… stopped answering my calls. One morning, I woke up to a text: *"Lo siento. No puedo."* I’m sorry. I can’t. No explanation. No goodbyes. Just the cold weight of his absence.

I sat on the edge of my bed and stared at my reflection in the mirror. *Lucía.* The name felt like a cage. I wanted to scream it, to tear it off my skin. But I couldn’t. It was mine. It was always mine.

That’s when I started writing.

At first, it was just letters—letters to him, letters to myself, letters to the girl I used to be. I wrote about the way his voice sounded when he laughed, about the way his hands felt when he held mine. I wrote about my mother’s hands, calloused from years of cooking and cleaning, about my father’s voice, deep and rumbling like the sea. I wrote about *Lucía de la Cruz*, about the seamstress who stitched dreams into fabric.

One day, I realized I was writing a story. A story about a girl named *Luz*, who was named after a light she never saw. A light that had been taken from her.

I don’t know if Daniel ever reads what I write. I don’t know if he remembers my name anymore. But I do.

And I keep writing.

Because names aren’t just words. They’re the first stories we’re given. And sometimes, the only way to survive is to rewrite them.
